title: Stacks: representation, push, pop, peek and overflow/underflow
learningObjectives: Explain the last-in, first-out (LIFO) rule and identify the top element of a stack.
Represent a bounded stack using a C array and a count or top index with a documented invariant.
Implement push, pop, peek and is_empty operations with explicit success/failure results.
Prevent overflow before writing and underflow before reading or removing an element.
Compare fixed-capacity array stacks with dynamically allocated or linked implementations.
Test stack behaviour on empty, one-item, full and repeated push/pop sequences.

understand.concept: A stack is an abstract data type that follows last-in, first-out (LIFO): the most recently pushed item is the first one popped. Its basic operations are push, pop and peek. A bounded array implementation stores elements in an array and tracks how many are currently present.
understand.whyItMatters: Stacks are used in expression evaluation, undo history, parsing, depth-first traversal and function-call management. Their simple interface is useful only when empty and full conditions are handled correctly.
understand.analogy: A stack of trays: a new tray is placed on top, and the top tray is the first one removed.
understand.analogyLimit: A software stack may have a fixed capacity or dynamic allocation and is not necessarily the same as the machine call stack. The tray analogy does not model memory allocation or error reporting.

explain.narrative:
For an array stack, store the number of elements in count. The invariant is 0 <= count <= capacity; when count is nonzero, the top item is data[count - 1]. Push first checks count < capacity, writes data[count], then increments count. Pop first checks count > 0, optionally copies data[count - 1] to the caller, then decrements count. Peek reads data[count - 1] without changing count.

Use size_t for capacity and count. Return a status such as bool to distinguish success from full or empty; do not use a valid data value as an error sentinel unless the interface explicitly reserves it. Check pointer arguments before dereferencing them. A fixed-capacity stack does not allocate memory, but callers must decide what to do when it is full.

A linked stack can grow by allocating nodes, but each push can fail and every successful allocation needs a matching release. The LIFO interface stays the same while the representation changes. Test empty pop/peek, exactly-full push, one-more-than-capacity push and interleaved operations.

examples.title: A bounded array stack with safe operations
examples.explanation: count records the number of stored values. Push checks capacity before writing; pop checks nonempty state before decrementing and reading the former top. A failed operation leaves the stack unchanged.

examples.title: Peek reads without removing the top item
examples.explanation: Peek uses count - 1 only after checking count is nonzero. It copies the top value to the output and does not modify the stack. The caller remains responsible for providing an array that actually contains count elements.

practise.guidedTask: Start with an empty stack. Trace push(4), push(9), peek, pop, pop and pop again. Record count and the top value after every operation, including the final underflow.
practise.independentTask: Implement a fixed-capacity stack of integers with push, pop, peek and is_empty. Test full and empty cases, null output pointers and verify that failed operations do not change the stack.
hints: With count elements, the top index is count - 1 only when count > 0.
Check capacity before writing to the array.
Check nonempty state before reading or decrementing the top.
A failed push or pop should leave the stack state unchanged.
Use a separate status result rather than reserving an ordinary integer as an error marker.
A dynamically allocated stack also needs a clear ownership and cleanup policy.

questions.explanation: The newest item is at the top and is removed first.

questions.prompt: For a stack represented by an array and count, where is the top item when count is greater than zero?
questions.explanation: The occupied indices are 0 through count - 1.

questions.prompt: What must push check before writing to a bounded stack?
options: That count is less than capacity
That count is already equal to capacity
That the stack is empty only
That the new value is nonzero
questions.answer: That count is less than capacity
questions.explanation: Writing when count equals capacity would access one past the valid array range.

options: Attempting to remove or inspect an item when the stack is empty
Attempting to push when the stack is full
questions.answer: Attempting to remove or inspect an item when the stack is empty
questions.explanation: Pop and peek require at least one stored element.

questions.prompt: What should happen when a push fails because the stack is full?
options: The stack remains unchanged and the caller receives a failure indication
The program writes beyond the array
The oldest element is silently overwritten
questions.answer: The stack remains unchanged and the caller receives a failure indication
questions.explanation: A clear failure result and unchanged state preserve the stack invariant.
